cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
A capacitor separates charge between conductors.
In our simple two plate model, one plate carries plus Q and the other minus Q.
The pair can have zero net charge while still storing electrical energy.
When we say the charge on the capacitor is Q, we mean the magnitude on one
plate, not twice that magnitude.
Capacitance is charge magnitude divided by the potential difference magnitude
between the conductors.
One farad means one coulomb per volt.
It tells us how much separated charge this arrangement holds for a given
voltage.
For an ideal linear capacitor with fixed geometry and material, capacitance
doesn't increase just because we apply a higher voltage.
Charge increases in the same ratio.
If capacitance is three microfarads and voltage is four volts, each plate
carries twelve microcoulombs in magnitude.
Double voltage to eight volts and charge becomes twenty four microcoulombs,
while capacitance remains three microfarads.
A microfarad is one millionth of a farad, whereas a picofarad is one
trillionth.
Keep those prefixes straight.
In electrostatic equilibrium the conducting plates are each equipotential, and
field within their conducting material is zero.
The insulating gap can still have a field.
Real capacitors have leakage and voltage limits, so this ideal linear model
has
a range of validity.
For JEE, first identify the two conductors, the voltage between them and what
Q
represents before applying the ratio.
Let's derive the parallel plate result rather than treating it as magic.
Take large opposite plates with charge magnitudes Q, area A and separation d,
with vacuum in the gap.
Well away from the edges, the combined field is approximately Q divided by
epsilon zero times area.
Potential difference magnitude is field times separation.
Divide Q by that potential difference, and capacitance becomes epsilon zero
times area divided by separation.
Charge cancels, because the geometry sets the ratio.
Bigger plates spread a given charge over more area and reduce the voltage
needed to hold it.
Bringing plates closer also lowers that voltage, increasing capacitance.
Use area zero point zero two square meters and separation one millimeter.
With epsilon zero equal to eight point eight five times ten to the minus
twelve, capacitance is one hundred and seventy seven picofarads.
At twelve volts the gap field is twelve thousand newtons per coulomb.
This model ignores edge fringing and assumes the gap is small relative to
plate
dimensions.
If a uniform linear dielectric completely fills the gap, multiply the vacuum
capacitance by its relative permittivity, kappa.
Partial filling requires a different geometry calculation; don't apply that
multiplier to the entire capacitor automatically.
Also, changing separation has different consequences depending on whether a
battery maintains voltage or whether the disconnected plates retain their
charge.
We'll use that fixed quantity reasoning throughout the rest of this class.
In a network, identify connected nodes rather than relying on how close
symbols
look on the page.
Capacitors are in parallel when both connect across the same two nodes.
They share voltage, so total separated charge is the sum of each capacitance
times that voltage.
Equivalent capacitance is the sum.
Two and three microfarads in parallel across ten volts give five microfarads
overall, with charges twenty and thirty microcoulombs.
Now connect the two capacitors in a simple series chain that starts uncharged,
with an isolated neutral intermediate node.
The plate charge magnitudes are equal.
Their voltage drops add, so the reciprocal of equivalent capacitance is the
sum
of the individual reciprocals.
Two and three microfarads in series give one point two microfarads.
Across ten volts, each capacitor carries twelve microcoulombs in magnitude.
Their voltages are six volts across the two microfarad capacitor and four
volts
across the three microfarad capacitor.
The smaller capacitance gets the larger voltage, because voltage equals the
common charge divided by capacitance.
Pause and check: six plus four returns the applied ten volts.
Series equivalent capacitance is smaller than either component; parallel
equivalent is larger than either.
If an internal node already has net charge or another connection, the simple
equal charge assumption may fail.
For more complicated JEE networks, label nodes, simplify valid series or
parallel groups, and then work backward to recover individual charges and
voltages.
Why is stored energy one half Q V instead of Q V?
While charging an initially uncharged ideal capacitor, the voltage rises from
zero to its final value.
Each small added charge needs work equal to the voltage at that moment times
the added charge.
Integrating those contributions gives Q squared divided by twice capacitance.
Substitute Q equals C V to get one half C V squared, or one half Q V.
These are equivalent expressions, not three different kinds of energy.
For two microfarads at ten volts, stored energy is one hundred microjoules and
charge is twenty microcoulombs.
If this capacitor stays disconnected with no leakage and its plate separation
doubles, capacitance halves.
Charge stays fixed, so energy doubles and voltage doubles.
An external agent must do work to pull the attracting plates apart.
If instead an ideal battery holds the voltage at ten volts while separation
doubles, capacitance halves, plate charge halves and stored energy halves.
In that case charge flows back toward the source, and the source belongs in
the
energy account.
Don't infer mechanical work from the capacitor energy change alone.
In vacuum, the field energy per unit volume is one half epsilon zero times
field squared.
For the ideal parallel plate geometry, multiplying by the gap volume
reproduces
the capacitor energy.
Your formula choice should follow the constraint, not whichever expression
looks shortest.
A dielectric is an insulating material whose charges respond to the electric
field through polarization.
Opposite bound charges appear near its faces.
They are not the same as freely conducting charges moving across the gap.
With fixed free plate charge, polarization reduces the gap field and voltage,
so the ratio Q over V increases.
Let's completely fill a capacitor's gap with a uniform linear dielectric of
kappa three, keeping plate geometry unchanged.
Start with two microfarads at ten volts: charge twenty microcoulombs and
energy
one hundred microjoules.
Disconnect the battery first, assuming no leakage.
Capacitance becomes six microfarads, charge remains twenty microcoulombs,
voltage becomes about three point three three volts, and energy becomes about
thirty three point three microjoules.
The energy reduction is available for mechanical work and any losses; it has
not vanished.
Now repeat from the same initial state but keep the ideal ten volt battery
connected.
Capacitance still becomes six microfarads, but voltage stays ten volts.
Charge increases to sixty microcoulombs and stored energy to three hundred
microjoules.
The battery supplies additional energy, so the increased capacitor energy does
not contradict attraction pulling the dielectric inward.
With fixed gap and fixed voltage, the average gap field stays V over d; the
battery's extra free charge compensates for polarization.
Real materials also have dielectric breakdown limits.
Our final checklist is: state the geometry, name the material model, identify
whether Q or V is fixed, then calculate capacitance, charge, voltage and
energy
consistently.
